extracted.intended_audience: Habitat for Humanity communications staff, affiliate PR/marketing writers, and press officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting press releases, social posts, blog posts and other communications consistent with the U.S. Habitat for Humanity brand narrative and messaging. Focuses on voice, language choices, story selection, facts, calls to action, and presentation of organizational vs. program identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand primacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct statements and sentences so that Habitat (the brand) is always the primary, most-referenced brand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual programs, events, initiatives, etc., are not brands unto themselves and should be consistently presented as part of Habitat for Humanity’s overall work. If you’re saying program names as often as or more than you’re saying “Habitat for Humanity,” reset. DO give primary placement to the Habitat for Humanity brand; DON’T accidentally create the impression that individual programs are the brands to be remembered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shorthand poverty phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful when using phrases like “poverty housing,” “path out of poverty” or “break the cycle of poverty.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a general audience, these aren’t the most easily understood or universal ways to describe need or Habitat’s impact. Instead, message: Habitat works to eliminate barriers to a better, healthier, more financially stable life. Use language that describes outcomes for families rather than shorthand poverty phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use faith references carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge Habitat’s Christian roots but avoid emphasizing faith connections in general-public communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus groups found mention of Habitat’s connection to a specific faith can be perceived as exclusionary. Use direct quotes from homeowners/volunteers that contain faith references when appropriate, but otherwise use faith language sparingly so as not to alienate general audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay advocacy messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid surfacing advocacy, lobbying or policy details early in general conversations about Habitat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General audiences are often turned off by early discussion of lobbying/politics and prefer emotional connection. Save complex policy details for deeper conversations; after a person has a foundation of knowledge, then ask for support for advocacy and policy efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use facts to show individual impact (not puffery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully choose facts to demonstrate how Habitat helps individuals and families; avoid large aggregate numbers that feel like puffery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People have trouble putting big numbers in perspective. Prefer facts that show homeowner outcomes and empowerment (high-performing facts) rather than aggregate totals or vaguer language (lower-performing facts). Examples of high-performing facts: children of homeowners are 116% more likely to graduate college; foreclosure rate on Habitat houses <2% annually. Lower-performing facts: large totals presented without a human face (e.g., “Over 1.6 million families have been impacted since 1976”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer homeowner-centered facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame facts so homeowner families—not the organization—are the primary actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistics that make it easy for people to see the individual (e.g., outcomes for families and children). Avoid facts that focus on the organization as the actor or that are overly aggregated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always include a call to action
rubrics_metrics.description: Never end a story without a direct call to action to help more families build strength, stability and independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls to action should regularly solicit financial support, voices and/or time. Keep language simple and high-level, offer specific avenues to dig deeper, and be explicit — ask directly for money, time, or voice as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bite-sized donation asks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use small, specific donation examples to motivate giving (e.g., $20 a month).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bite-sized currencies help people realize everyone can make a difference and make the ask feel doable. Include clear examples of what small gifts accomplish when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize volunteers alongside donations
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when emphasizing financial donations, remember volunteers are the heart, soul and muscle behind Habitat’s efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly solicit both time and money in communications and acknowledge volunteer contributions; don’t shift entirely to donations at the expense of volunteer recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline and opening paragraph priorities for releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead with lasting, meaningful outcomes (strength, stability, shelter) in headlines and opening paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In press releases and major announcements, emphasize the outcomes families experience. For annual reports, aggregate numbers are appropriate but pair them immediately with a face/story so numbers don’t stand alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use photographs/captions to humanize data
rubrics_metrics.description: Pair large numbers with photos and captions that put a face to the work so the aggregate number doesn’t stand alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A photo and caption can almost immediately humanize a large number and make the data feel real and relatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place US information first for US audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting regional breakdowns for a U.S.-based audience, place U.S. and Canada information first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many among the U.S.-based audience prioritize seeing U.S. information first; structure charts/tables accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Habitat language and vision phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use approved vision and message phrases such as “A world where everyone has a decent place to live” and “Building strength, stability, self-reliance and shelter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the highest-level messaging phrase in callouts, merchandise, or when that phrase is the sole message. ‘Independence’ is an acceptable synonym for ‘self-reliance.’ In places where ‘shelter’ might confuse, use ‘affordable homeownership.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Build on the 'everyone' construct
rubrics_metrics.description: Creatively use structures like “Everyone, every donation, every helping hand...” to reinforce inclusivity and make housing need relatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided (Everyone needs a foundation to build a future; Every donation helps a family help themselves) should be used to help individuals find their place in the effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred adjectival usage: 'decent and affordable'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use “decent and affordable place to call home” instead of “simple, decent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public perceptions of “simple” vary and often disrupt the intended narrative, especially when paired with photos. Prefer “decent and affordable.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic phrasing order
rubrics_metrics.description: When referencing scope, say “In your community and around the world.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ordering reassures donors we build locally first and also work internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice: first-person plural
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to Habitat in the first-person plural (we, our) where appropriate to give a confident, inclusive, human voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicators are the living embodiment of the organization; use ‘we’ rather than reporting in an outside voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer present tense
rubrics_metrics.description: Write in the present tense whenever appropriate to make stories feel immediate and dynamic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present tense combined with rich descriptions engages readers and gives a 'you are there' feeling. Use past tense only where chronology requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name usage & first reference rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use full organization names in first reference for general audiences; only use HFH/HFHI internally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always use “Habitat for Humanity” with affiliate or national organization name on first reference (e.g., Habitat for Humanity of Charlotte; Habitat for Humanity Guatemala). “Habitat” with affiliate/nation name is acceptable subsequently. HFH/HFHI only for internal documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal name usage conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred usage is homeowner’s first name only in Habitat-produced publications; volunteers/supporters get full name on first reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgment calls may vary; always prioritize respect, dignity and privacy of homeowners. Use full names for volunteers/supporters on first reference, then first name thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'partner' as a verb; homeowner descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'partner' as a verb (families partner with Habitat) and use 'future homeowners' vs 'homeowners' appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Future homeowners’ refers to families accepted to build and working on sweat equity; use 'homeowners' after dedication or for families who partner for repairs. In some contexts 'homebuyers' is acceptable when emphasizing financial education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stigmatizing language about poverty
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to circumstances not people: use phrases like 'people living in poor conditions' or 'people in the world’s poorest places' rather than 'poor people' or 'poor neighborhoods.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saying 'poor people' distances and stigmatizes; frame poverty as a circumstance to encourage empathy and inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make homeowners active in storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Write that Habitat builds 'with' families and 'alongside' families; emphasize homeowners' agency in stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say volunteers help families raise walls rather than 'volunteers help raise the walls of Jane Doe’s house.' Use 'families partner with Habitat' instead of 'Habitat partners with families.' DON’T say we build 'for' families or that families 'get' Habitat houses when you can emphasize building/partnership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid value judgments about families
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not characterize families using words like 'deserving' or 'hardworking.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inclusive statements such as 'everyone deserves a decent place to live' rather than dividing people into groups. Avoid language that introduces unintentional value judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish family eligibility criteria in communications
rubrics_metrics.description: When relevant, emphasize the criteria that establish a family's participation: need for decent and affordable housing, willingness to partner, and ability to repay an affordable mortgage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this when explaining the partnership model—clarifies that homeowners are active participants who meet standards rather than passive recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story selection: specificity and solvability
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell moving, specific stories about individuals or families and make the story feel solvable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paint a picture with concrete details that make it easy for readers to relate and imagine themselves in similar situations. Pick stories that illustrate core themes (strength, stability, self-reliance). Don't tell every story—choose those with elements that best demonstrate the brand platform; repetition is reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strong, clear quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Include direct quotes that reinforce main messaging points of strength, stability and self-reliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a quote is too general or vague, don’t be afraid to publish a story without a quote. Prioritize quotes that add authenticity and emotional resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core themes to highlight
rubrics_metrics.description: Center communications around the core themes: strength, stability, self-reliance (and shelter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use family and volunteer stories to draw out examples of these themes (e.g., how a decent home enables a parent to feel proud and provide; ramps enable dignity and independence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate and links drive engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use boilerplate language and links (e.g., to the annual report and donation pages) to drive readers to the website where family stories and donation asks live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear links and a concise boilerplate in press releases to provide next steps and additional context for interested readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate numbers belong in annual reports or deeper channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Large aggregate statistics (e.g., '6.8 million people impacted since 1976') are best used in annual reports or contexts where readers expect high-level metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you do use aggregate numbers in communications, pair them with a human story and photo to avoid the perception of puffery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid antiquated or internally resonant historical jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t use historical words/phrases that lack resonance with a general audience (examples: habititis, oyez, theology of the hammer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Celebrate history where appropriate, but quote current leaders unless referring to a clear historical context. Keep tone consistent with the brand personality in this guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release structure examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow structure shown in sample press release: headline emphasizing outcomes, lead paragraph with core numbers framed by human impact, CEO quote highlighting outcomes, regional chart ordered for audience, and supporting boilerplate/link.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sample as a template: put outcome-focused headline and lead, add a quote from leadership that ties to family outcomes, include a table/chart with region-first ordering appropriate to audience, and end with boilerplate and links to reports/donation pages.
